profilePeriod: Career emphasis on deputy premiership 2007–2010 and premiership 2010–2013, with explicitly dated later positions on marriage equality and education through October 2025; sources checked September 2026.
scopeNote: Answers are editorial simulations of documented political principles, not a questionnaire completed by the person. Brazil-specific statements are interpreted in the analogous home-country context. Modern hypothetical technologies require inference.

sources.title: National Archives: Julia Gillard during office
sources.evidence: Minority government formed by parliamentary negotiation; departure after losing caucus ballot. NBN, carbon pricing, mining tax, NDIS and needs-based school funding were enacted. Afghanistan deployment continued. NDIS directed public funding to individual choice of services.

sources.title: A better deal for patients
sources.evidence: National standards and pooled hospital funding combined with state partnership and greater local hospital and clinical control. Commonwealth did not seek to take back state GST revenue.

sources.title: National curriculum press conference
sources.evidence: Gillard insisted on a national curriculum as a condition of extra school funding. She opposed state fragmentation while supporting consultation, evidence and local teachers.

sources.title: Michael Kirby Oration
sources.evidence: Defended parliamentary democratic decision-making against substituting plebiscites for legislative responsibility; explicitly changed to support same-sex marriage. Earlier opposition reflected her preference for a new civil-union institution, not religious faith.

sources.title: National Plan to Tackle Gangs, Organised Crime and the Illegal Firearms Market
sources.evidence: Sought state referrals for national anti-gang and unexplained-wealth laws, and stronger controls against firearms trafficking. Supports enforcement and national coordination, not abolition of constitutional state institutions.

sources.title: Carr joins calls for rethink of drugs laws
sources.evidence: Gillard rejected decriminalisation and treated drugs as destructive to lives and families, alongside the need for treatment.

sources.title: Interview, Australian Agenda
sources.evidence: Gillard understood end-of-life choice but found safeguards inadequate. Defended UN-authorised protection of Libyan civilians. Described cultural traditionalism (thrift, duty, discipline), not religious belief; supported knowledge of Bible stories as cultural literacy.

sources.title: Australian Multicultural Council lecture
sources.evidence: Celebrated multiculturalism and rights to retain language, religion and customs, paired with learning English, work, respect for Australian heritage, gender equality, democracy and rule of law.

sources.title: Refugee program increased to 20,000 places
sources.evidence: Raised humanitarian intake to 20,000 for 2012–13 and funded UNHCR capacity building.

sources.title: Human Rights Commission: detention policy 2004–2014
sources.evidence: Gillard reintroduced offshore processing in 2012: Nauru transfers in September and Manus in November. The absolute no-settlement rule announced in July 2013 was Rudd’s, and is not attributed to Gillard.

sources.title: Australia’s National Security Beyond the 9/11 Decade
sources.evidence: Strong military and US alliance, Afghan training and possible special-forces contribution, regional engagement and cyber coordination; simultaneously defended multilateral rules, diplomacy, rights and peaceful dispute settlement. National interests remain distinctively Australian.

sources.title: Doorstop interview Sydney
sources.evidence: Affirmed Reserve Bank independence while discussing exchange-rate pressures and jobs.

sources.title: Joint communiqué with Thai prime minister
sources.evidence: Supported expanded trade and investment, review of TAFTA and reduction of trade impediments, plus the regional free-trade agenda.

sources.title: Holden Cruze launch
sources.evidence: Welcomed Australian-made Holden Cruze backed by $149 million public investment in the New Car Plan; strategic manufacturing assistance coexists with trade liberalisation.

sources.title: Prime Minister puts her faith in chaplaincy
sources.evidence: Publicly atheist and respectful of believers; extended school chaplaincy funding. Irreligiosity does not imply removing all religious services or traditions.

sources.title: Gillard admits she got it wrong on marriage equality
sources.evidence: Reaffirmed marriage-equality support and acknowledged her earlier parliamentary opposition was wrong.

sources.title: University of Sydney occasional address
sources.evidence: Defended access to education, girls’ opportunities, secular admissions and effective DEI. Criticised authoritarian politics, concentrated wealth and backlash against gender equality. Recognised opportunities and risks of AI.

sources.title: Women Deliver speech reported by SBS
sources.evidence: Current-date discovery confirms continuing gender-equality advocacy. Used only as freshness check: substantive profile period remains the existing October 2025 cutoff.

sources.title: Press conference on uranium and India
sources.evidence: Favoured uranium sales to India for jobs and strategic ties with safeguards, but considered domestic nuclear energy unnecessary given other resources and clean-energy alternatives.

sources.title: Great clean energy future address
sources.evidence: Used a carbon price and investment-driven technological transition toward cleaner energy, rather than rejecting industrial growth.

sources.title: Publisher: My Story ebook
sources.evidence: Publisher credits Julia Gillard as author and gives first ebook publication 24 September 2014. The work addresses her government, hung parliament, economic policy, education, disability reform and alliances; a qualifying political memoir.

facts: National curriculum imposed common requirements (2010).
Health reform paired national standards/funding with state and local control (2011).
National anti-gang coordination sought state referrals (2013).
estrutura.tension: Cooperative federalism with forceful Commonwealth policy leadership, not state abolition or secessionism.

facts: Parliamentary minority coalition and acceptance of leadership defeat (2010–13).
Explicit defence of representative democracy over plebiscites (2015).
representacao.tension: Strong reform leadership is not autocracy; she resists direct-democratic shortcuts as well as authoritarianism.

facts: Tough firearms and anti-gang enforcement (2013).
Opposed drug decriminalisation (2012).
Euthanasia safeguard objections (2011).
poder.tension: Security measures and paternalistic health rules coexist with rule-of-law and political rights; not libertarian or totalitarian.

facts: Cultural and language pluralism explicitly defended (2012).
Required English and equal rights; expanded refugee intake alongside offshore processing (2012).
imigracao.tension: Civic integration and controlled asylum channels must not be confused with ethnic exclusion or open borders.

facts: Continued Afghan military engagement and supported strong defence/US alliance (2010–13).
Diplomacy and peaceful multilateral order stressed in 2013.
diplomacia.tension: Credible armed defence plus diplomacy, not pacifist disarmament or unrestricted preventive war.

facts: National-interest-led regional engagement and Afghan training were defended (2013).
Supported international institutions and rules, not unconditional neutrality.
intervencao.tension: Active allied middle power; rejects both isolationism and coercive domination of neighbours.

facts: NDIS public insurance with individual choice and needs-based education (2013).
Public broadband and public hospitals coexist with market incentives (2011).
economia.tension: Mixed economy and universal services do not entail collectivising firms or abolishing private property.

facts: Carbon price, mining tax and public investment (2011–13).
Independent Reserve Bank explicitly respected (2012).
Manufacturing subsidy to Holden (2011).
controle.tension: Regulation and social protection alongside competition, independent money and fiscal constraints; no full command economy.

facts: Promoted TAFTA, investment and regional trade expansion (2012).
Subsidised car production domestically (2011).
comercio.tension: Open trade with selective industry support, not autarky or blanket tariff protection.

facts: Atheist yet funded chaplaincy and recognised religious contribution (2010).
Secular education access praised in 2025.
religiao.tension: Secular personal/public reasoning plus accommodation of religious citizens, not militant erasure.

facts: Gender equality and DEI affirmed (2012, 2025).
Marriage equality supported in 2015 and reaffirmed 2023 after earlier opposition.
moral.tension: Preserve dated reversal; do not portray her premiership as having enacted marriage equality or infer all lifestyle issues from feminism.

facts: NBN and clean-energy industrial innovation supported (2011).
Domestic nuclear viewed as unnecessary while uranium exports supported (2011).
Recognised AI opportunities and risks (2025).
tecnologia.tension: Scientific modernisation bounded by regulation and environmental protection; no evidence for unlimited human enhancement.

uncertainties: A simulated answer is an inference, not a quotation or recorded response. Questions naming Brazil are interpreted through analogous Australian institutions and principles.
Profile period is preserved verbatim; 2026 reporting was checked for description freshness and is not silently substituted for historical policies.

No direct position was verified on neural augmentation, designer embryos, cultivated meat, cryptocurrency competition, facial recognition, inheritance tax or polyamory; those answers use bounded inference from regulated scientific progress, civic liberties and mixed-economy practice.
No verified Brazilian edition of My Story was located in dedicated Portuguese-title searches; retain original title rather than invent a translation.
Official announcements evidence commitments, not proof of all implementation outcomes.
